name: Pop Punk
about: Pop punk keeps punk's speed and buzzsaw guitars but writes the choruses rock radio would want, a line that runs from the Ramones and Buzzcocks through the Descendents, whose 1982 debut about girls, food and growing up fixed the template. Berkeley's Lookout! label and the Gilman Street club bred Green Day, Screeching Weasel and Mr. T Experience in the late 1980s, and in 1994 Dookie and The Offspring's Smash took the sound to the stadiums. Blink-182 added toilet humor and glossy production at the end of the decade, New Found Glory and Sum 41 followed, and by the mid-2000s Fall Out Boy and Paramore had merged it with emo. The 2010s revival around The Wonder Years and Joyce Manor returned it to small rooms and plain feeling.

artists.name: Buzzcocks
artists.why: wrote the punk love song's rulebook

artists.name: Green Day
artists.why: Gilman Street to twenty million copies

artists.name: blink-182
artists.why: glossy San Diego juvenilia, hugely influential

artists.name: Fall Out Boy
artists.why: merged the sound with emo and pop

albums.title: Rocket to Russia
albums.why: Sheena Is a Punk Rocker and Rockaway Beach made the third album the Ramones' most tuneful and best-produced, their bubblegum side at full strength.

albums.title: Singles Going Steady
albums.why: The American compilation of the Manchester band's singles is where the canon lives, with Ever Fallen in Love and What Do I Get? as the pop-punk standard.

albums.title: The Undertones
albums.why: Teenage Kicks and a dozen songs about girls and chocolate, sung in Feargal Sharkey's quaver, made the most innocent and tuneful record of British punk.

albums.title: Milo Goes to College
albums.why: Fifteen songs in twenty-two minutes about girls, parents and suburban boredom, with Bill Stevenson's drumming, set the pop-punk template for forty years.

albums.title: My Brain Hurts
albums.why: Ben Weasel's Ramones worship found its own voice on the Chicago band's third album, the Lookout! era's sharpest and most quotable record.

albums.title: Dookie
albums.why: Basket Case and Longview, played with Berkeley sloppiness and Beatles hooks, sold twenty million copies and put punk on MTV for a decade.

albums.title: Smash
albums.why: Come Out and Play and Self Esteem made the best-selling independent album of its time and carried Epitaph's melodic punk to the suburbs.

albums.title: Everything Sucks
albums.why: Milo Aukerman's return after nine years delivered the band's most consistent set of fast, funny, sad songs, with I'm the One and the title track up front.

albums.title: Love Is Dead
albums.why: Dr. Frank's wordy, self-deprecating love songs on the Berkeley band's best album made pop punk literate without making it less catchy.

albums.title: Don't Back Down
albums.why: Joe Queer's Beach Boys fixation and Ramones chords on the band's cleanest-sounding record made the New Hampshire trio's most enduring album.

albums.title: Jersey's Best Dancers
albums.why: Ari Katz's pleading vocals over hardcore-speed melody on the New Jersey band's final 1990s album became the model for the next decade's scene.

albums.title: Midwestern Songs of the Americas
albums.why: Minneapolis's gruff, political pop punk at its tightest, with Doublewhiskeycokenoice setting the standard for the Fest-era bands that followed.

albums.title: Goddamnit
albums.why: Matt Skiba and Dan Andriano's Chicago debut mixed morbid romance and drinking songs into pop punk's darkest and most durable early record.

albums.title: Enema of the State
albums.why: Jerry Finn's glossy production and Travis Barker's drums turned the trio's dirty jokes into All the Small Things and the sound of 2000s radio.

albums.title: Through Being Cool
albums.why: Chris Conley's teenage lyrics about leaving town, delivered at Lifetime speed, made the New Jersey record that bridged pop punk and emo.

albums.title: Bleed American
albums.why: The Middle and Sweetness made the Arizona band's self-financed fourth album the moment emo-leaning pop punk became unavoidable on the radio.

albums.title: All Killer No Filler
albums.why: Fat Lip and In Too Deep made the Ontario band's debut the sharpest of the post-blink wave, with metal riffs and rap verses thrown in for fun.

albums.title: Sticks and Stones
albums.why: My Friends Over You and Jordan Pundik's nasal yearning defined the Warped Tour's early-2000s sound more completely than any other record.

albums.title: American Idiot
albums.why: A punk rock opera about the Bush years with nine-minute suites, it revived the band's career, won a Grammy and became a Broadway musical.

albums.title: From Under the Cork Tree
albums.why: Pete Wentz's run-on titles and Patrick Stump's soul-trained voice on Sugar, We're Goin Down made emo-pop punk the sound of the mid-2000s charts.

albums.title: Riot!
albums.why: Misery Business and Hayley Williams's voice made the Franklin, Tennessee band the Warped Tour's biggest act and the genre's most durable 2000s export.

albums.title: Joyce Manor
albums.why: Ten songs in under nineteen minutes, with Constant Headache the anthem, made the Torrance band's debut the 2010s revival's most economical classic.

albums.title: The Greatest Generation
albums.why: Dan Campbell's suburban Philadelphia grief and ambition, with a seven-minute closer, made the earnest 2010s pop punk revival's most complete album.

albums.title: The Dream Is Over
albums.why: Stefan Babcock's shredded vocal cords and the Toronto band's gang choruses on If This Tour Doesn't Kill You, I Will made the decade's most cathartic pop punk record.
